questions.question: Why is a raw uploaded video transcoded into multiple resolutions?
options: To add watermarks and copyright protection
To serve viewers with different devices and bandwidth levels the best quality they can handle
To reduce the total storage required
To convert all videos to a single universal format
questions.explanation: Different viewers have different bandwidth and device capabilities. A mobile user on 3G needs 360p; a 4K TV on fiber needs 2160p. Transcoding into multiple resolutions ensures every viewer gets the best experience their connection can support.

questions.question: What is Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (ABR)?
options: A technique that compresses video to a fixed bitrate
A method where the player dynamically switches video quality segment-by-segment based on current bandwidth
A server-side algorithm that reduces video resolution permanently
A protocol that increases upload speed for content creators
questions.explanation: ABR splits video into small segments (2-10 seconds) encoded at multiple quality levels. The player continuously monitors available bandwidth and selects the highest quality each segment can be delivered at, switching seamlessly as conditions change.

questions.question: What role does a CDN play in video streaming?
options: It transcodes videos into different formats
It caches video segments at edge locations worldwide to reduce latency for viewers
It compresses videos to reduce file size
It handles user authentication for premium content
questions.explanation: A CDN caches video segments at edge servers distributed globally. A viewer in Tokyo fetches segments from a nearby edge server rather than the origin data center in the US, dramatically reducing latency and improving playback quality.

questions.question: Why do video upload services support chunked, resumable uploads?
options: To allow multiple users to upload the same video simultaneously
Because large video files risk connection drops; resumability prevents restarting the entire upload
To split the video into segments for ABR streaming
To encrypt each chunk separately for security
questions.explanation: Video files can be gigabytes in size. On unreliable connections, a full upload might fail near completion. Chunked resumable uploads allow the client to resume from the last successfully uploaded chunk rather than starting over.

questions.question: How does parallelizing transcoding reduce processing time?
options: By using faster CPUs on a single machine
By splitting the video into segments, transcoding each on different machines simultaneously, then stitching results
By skipping certain frames to reduce the work
By only transcoding the audio track in parallel
questions.explanation: A two-hour video is split into many short segments. Each segment is transcoded independently on different machines (a DAG pipeline). This parallelism can turn hours of transcoding into minutes, then the segments are stitched back together.

questions.question: What is an HLS manifest file and what information does it contain?
options: A binary file containing the video codec configuration
A text file listing available quality levels and the URLs of each video segment at each quality
A database index for fast video search
A DRM license file for content protection
questions.explanation: An HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) manifest (.m3u8) is a text playlist that lists all available quality levels (bitrates/resolutions) and the URLs for each video segment at each quality. The player parses this manifest to know which segments to request.

questions.question: How does Netflix optimize CDN usage for content it knows will be popular?
options: It reduces the video quality of popular content to save bandwidth
It pre-positions popular content at edge locations before peak viewing hours
It limits the number of concurrent viewers per title
It serves popular content only from the origin data center
questions.explanation: Netflix uses predictive pre-positioning (called Open Connect) to push popular titles to edge servers during off-peak hours. When peak viewing starts, content is already cached at the edge, eliminating origin fetches and reducing latency.

questions.question: What is the key architectural difference between live streaming and video-on-demand streaming?
options: Live streaming doesn't use CDNs
Live streaming requires real-time transcoding and immediate CDN push since content cannot be pre-processed
Video-on-demand doesn't need transcoding
Live streaming uses higher resolution than video-on-demand
questions.explanation: VOD content is transcoded in advance and cached. Live streaming must transcode in real-time as the stream arrives and push segments to CDN edges immediately. This means less time for optimization and typically 5-30 seconds of latency.

questions.question: A video platform stores each video in 5 resolutions and 2 codecs. A 10-minute video at 1080p is 1GB raw. Total storage per video after transcoding is approximately?
options: 1 GB (same as raw)
10 GB (one per resolution-codec combination)
Approximately 3-4 GB (lower resolutions are proportionally smaller)
50 GB
questions.explanation: Lower resolutions require much less storage (240p might be 5% of 1080p size). With 5 resolutions (e.g., 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) in 2 codecs, the total is roughly 3-4x the 1080p size, not 10x, because lower resolutions contribute much less data.

questions.question: A live sports event has 10 million concurrent viewers. Each viewer consumes 5 Mbps. Without a CDN, all traffic hits the origin. What bandwidth would the origin need?
options: 50 Gbps
500 Gbps
5 Tbps
50 Tbps
questions.explanation: 10 million viewers x 5 Mbps = 50 million Mbps = 50 Tbps. This is physically impossible from a single origin. This is exactly why CDNs are essential — they distribute the load across thousands of edge servers, each serving a fraction of viewers.
